questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go to a place in Europe where I could more or less speak the language with the possibility of also studying in that language.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: On a personal level I have had a really good time, but the university didn't make it so.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Stockholm University offers some information but on many different webpages - it can be a bit of a jungle to find the correct information and your possibilities as a new international student. There wasn't a lot of introductions to the university itself - and the few possible introduction activities were at the same time as my classes. As a master's student I felt that I was pretty much on my own - perhaps it is different at BA-level.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Nothing really. I looked into Studentkåren and tried participating in some of their activities the first few weeks.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I have heard from other Swedes that have studied at other Swedish universities, that they focus a lot on introduction programmes each semester - even for the international students. I thought the information was messy and at times unclear. I did however have a kind international coordinator at my "home department" (department of swedish and bilingualism) that sent me my personal study information before the semester started.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I was really lucky through Facebook advertisements. I would recommend becoming a member of as many Stockholm housing FB-groups as possible and keeping an eye out up to half year before the semester. I had applied for all the student housing through the university but they couldn't offer me any housing. I know several people who experienced the same but also ended up having trouble finding anything privately. You have to be quick and make peace with the fact that you'll probably have to live outside the city center.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: The Tunnelbana system is really good and easy, so don't worry about having to live outside of the city center. If you can find a place close by a Tunnelbana station you'll get around the city easily and in no time! There is also a Tunnelbana station right by the university so it's very easy to get to campus.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Giving this a low rating as applications for student housing through the university opened pretty late - as I remember it opened in November as the semester started in January. Even though I applied for all the housing possibilities, they couldn't offer me any housing, and it seems they have nowhere near the amount of rooms that are required - luckily I was on the lookout privately at the same time.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There seemed to be a very big mix up during my registration, but I would say that it wasn't only Stockholm University (SU) that was the problem, but also my coordinator at UCPH. There was definitely miscommunication throughout which made a very stressful process to register.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
I received an e-mail from the coordinator at UCPH only a couple of days before the registration deadline saying something along the lines of "sorry for the short deadline". I had already looked into the courses I was interested in beforehand and I would recommend you do the same in case you are given as short a deadline as I was. Although I had prepared myself the short deadline was stressful as I had questions about the academic requirements stated in the course catalogue on
SU.se
and that left me very little time to get information from the guidance counsellors at SU.
After having registered and receiving a confirmation e-mail I expected everything to be settled. A few weeks later I received an e-mail Friday afternoon from my coordinator at UCPH, saying that he had received a message from SU saying I hadn't registered and if I wanted to secure my spot at SU I had until that Sunday the same weekend to send an application. This was again very stressful as I didn't expect to be able to get any guidance on a weekend and I couldn't understand why I had to apply again when I had already received confirmation on my registration.
In the end there had been miscommunication between SU and UCPH which lead to me receiving unnecessary messages about a re-application - my first registration was correct, but they had overlooked it apparently.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The guidance counsellors at SU were helpful although it was a little difficult to find the correct people to contact.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the courses I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Prepare yourself by looking at the available courses as you might not have a lot of time between receiving the registration information and the registration deadline. I was only allowed to choose courses from max. two different departments, so make sure you are aware of where the courses are being offered. The courses run in different "periods" - I had 2 x 7,5 ECTS in periode1 and 2 x 7,5 ECTS in periode2.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Much of the coursework was on Zoom which was very annoying as that meant that half of my studies were through a screen and not at the university. There were no corona restrictions, but apparently SU likes to offer online courses. When I registered for the courses they were described as being on campus, but were changed to online after my registration.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level was doable, but the amount of work in the different courses changed a lot!

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I prefer UCPH with bigger courses throughout the whole semester. Having the "block structure" meant that I never really got to know my classmates before we were moving on to the next courses. The online courses were only every second week, which meant that I had 3 hours of class one week and 5 hours the next; 3 hours every week at the university and 2 hours on a screen at home.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- Gender and post- colonialism in Latin America
- Sociolingvistik 1- allmän del
- Intercultural pragmatics
- Advanced Studies in Sociolinguistic Approaches to Bi- and multilingualism

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
The course in intercultural pragmatics and sociolinguistic approaches were very interesting, but the workload was pretty big. Unfortunately Intercultural Pragmatics was online.

I would not recommend the course Gender and Post-colonialism in Latin America unless you have extensive knowledge on the Latin American countries as the course was very descriptive about the places and their political statuses rather than theoretical.

Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Not necessarily an unexpected cost, but make sure to look into your phone subscription beforehand as you cannot register for a Swedish subscription unless you're registered at Skatteverket (folkeregister/adress). You can however get a SIM-card and credit at local shops, but you will have to put money on it once a month.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food (especially dairy and eggs) and alcohol is expensive. You also have to pay entry fees in all museums although some have student discounts.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The system is very different - you pay a membership to the Studentkår and they are at a Faculty level rather than Department levels.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you buy a membership (it's cheap) you can participate in lots of different activities. You can buy several memberships so you can participate in the different faculty clubs' activities - I bought a membership to both the humanities and the social sciences.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The Thursday bar at Café Bojan was fun sometimes

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Explore Södermalm and find your favourite local hangout spots. Find your local sunkpub to save money!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy as Danes and Swedes are very similar - be prepared for the fact that a lot of Swedish people do not understand a lot of Danish!

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I didn't get a lot of social possibilities out of my classes but I participated in some of the Studentkår-activities - I would say you have to throw yourself into it a couple of times even though it may be exhausting. I did however not really meet any local students - most are internationals.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
That you have to buy alcohol at Systembolaget and that the metro doesn't run in the night on week days. 

Not really a cultural thing but the winter is cold and the snow can be annoying. Swedish bread is always a tiny little bit sweet, which I find weird.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Again not really cultural but how Stockholm is similar to a lot of places (including CPH) but still its own in the best way. I appreciate the concepts of fika and lillördag.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Make sure you read up on your course possibilities and housing early on
2. Have proper winter clothes and good winter boots - preferably ones that can grip into the snow/ice
3. If you like me don't come to feel a real connection to the university, try to make peace with it and make your trip into a personal experience - do what you enjoy and remember that grades aren't everything (and won't even be transferred to UCPH). Better get what you can out of the experience rather than being frustrated that the university maybe isn't what you expected.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Make sure you have some money saved up as you may not receive your grant in time for the start of your exchange.
If you make sure to look into it early on you can find cheap train tickets between CPH and STHLM through
sj.se
.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Becoming familiar with the city and experiencing the seasons change from winter to spring to summer. Meeting new people and gaining life long memories.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Being on your own, feeling the stress of having to find friends, coming to terms with the university not being as I had hoped, the extreme price of butter and eggs.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
